File is missing a trailing newline at EOF (diff shows `\ No newline at end of file`). Most editors and Rust style guides (rustfmt) expect files to end with `\n`. Trivial, but worth a one-character fix.

Note: previously confirmed findings (function name `column_label` vs new `TaskStatus` parameter, doc-comment grammar nit "三 variant", and the reduced-but-sufficient test coverage) have already been acknowledged in the prior pass and are not repeated here.

Using `.parse().expect()` here introduces a panic-on-mismatch risk if `valid_status` and `parse` ever get out of sync (e.g., `valid_status` is edited to accept a wider set, or someone removes the earlier validation). Since the lock is already held here, a panic would propagate out of the HTTP handler thread. Consider factoring `valid_status` into a single `parse_status(s) -> Option<TaskStatus>` helper used once, so validation and parsing can never diverge. The `expect()` defense ("validated above") is a fragile cross-function invariant.

content: Same `.parse().expect()` pattern as in `create_task` — relies on a cross-function invariant that `validate_update_input` already called `valid_status`. If that validator is later relaxed or bypassed, the panic here will take down the handler. Prefer a single parse-and-validate helper used at the validation site and reuse the resulting enum.

`drop(_rmw)` works but reads awkwardly — the leading underscore conventionally signals "intentionally unused", yet the binding is consumed here. A scoped block makes the lock's lifetime visually obvious to readers and reviewers, and removes the need for the explicit `drop` plus the explanatory comment in three call sites.

The new doc comment on `SseWriterReg.hub_key` claims the counter is "跨进程单调" (monotonic across processes), but per `api_server.rs:60-62` the `EVENT_HUB_COUNTER` is explicitly **not** cross-process — it resets on restart. Only in-process monotonicity is guaranteed (and that's all the writers need, since they live entirely in-process and don't persist). Recommend rewording to "进程内单调递增（跨进程不保证）" to avoid misleading future readers.

`test_hub_key` uses `Ordering::SeqCst` for a simple monotonic ID counter. Since no other data is synchronized through this atomic (only uniqueness matters, not ordering relative to other memory operations), `Ordering::Relaxed` is the idiomatic choice for monotonic ID generators and avoids unnecessary memory barrier costs on weakly-ordered architectures.

content: New `pub` enum with hand-written `Serialize`/`Deserialize`, `FromStr`, `Display`, and `as_str` has no unit tests of its own. The doc comment makes a load-bearing claim ("wire format 与 ... 改 enum 前的 String 完全兼容,不需要迁移") that is exactly what a serde round-trip test would lock down — and the codebase clearly already exercises such contracts elsewhere (e.g. `task_out.rs` has `assert_eq!(obj["status"], obj["column"], ...)`). A small `#[cfg(test)] mod task_status_tests` covering: (a) each variant's `as_str` / `Display`, (b) `from_str` for valid + invalid + case-sensitivity (rejecting "TODO" etc.), (c) `serde_json::from_str::<TaskStatus>("\"doing\"")` round-trip, (d) full `Task` serde round-trip preserving the `column` string shape would be cheap insurance against future drift between the wire format and the enum.

The `col` shadowing at line 329 hides the original string from the eprintln branch. Suggest binding the raw value before parsing (e.g. `let raw = col; let col: TaskStatus = match raw.parse() { ... Err(e) => eprintln!("[db] 任务 {id} 的 col 值「{raw}」无法识别为 TaskStatus，按 Todo 兜底读取（原值未动）：{e}"), ... }`).

The `+ 1` here is inconsistent with `persisted()` below, which uses `EVENT_HUB_COUNTER.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst)` without the `+ 1`. Since `EVENT_HUB_COUNTER` already starts at 1 (to skip the 0 sentinel reserved by `API_HUB_KEY`), the first `new()` call returns `1 + 1 = 2` while the first `persisted()` call returns `1`. If a test creates a `new()` hub followed by a `persisted()` hub (or any mix in the same process), the IDs can collide (e.g. `new()` first → ID 2, then `persisted()` → also ID 2). It also contradicts the doc comment claiming "从 1 起跳" — `new()` actually skips 1. Drop the `+ 1` to match `persisted()` and the documented intent.

content: [high] `api_stop` no longer clears `api-enabled.flag`. The previous `api_stop_locked(.., clear_enabled: bool)` accepted `true` from `api_stop` and called `clear_enabled_flag(app)`; both the parameter and the in-body call were removed, and `api_stop_impl` does not invoke `clear_enabled_flag` either. The only remaining caller of `clear_enabled_flag` in the crate is `api_status` — and only for the dead-service edge case (`!enabled && g.is_some()`), which doesn't cover the normal stop path. A user-explicit API toggle-off via the Settings UI therefore leaves `runtime/flags/api-enabled.flag` set on disk, and the next app launch will auto-restore the API the user just disabled. Either restore the `clear_enabled_flag(&app)` call in `api_stop_impl` after `drop(g)` (matching the new "file I/O outside lock" convention), or pass a `clear_enabled` bool back from `api_stop_locked` so the caller can decide outside the lock.

[high] TOCTOU window between Phase 2 failure and Phase 3 re-acquiring `state.0`. A concurrent `api_start` can land in the gap: it reads the still-new token from disk, populates `g` with a service bound to `token_new`, and writes `api-enabled.flag`. When the recovery lock is taken, `api_start_locked` sees `g.is_some()` + `alive=true` and short-circuits returning `ApiInfo { token: Some(old_token) }` — but the running service is bound to `token_new`. The returned token no longer authenticates against the live service. Conversely a concurrent `api_stop` can empty `g`, leaving the recovery to restart a fresh service with `old_token` while the user wanted the API off. At minimum, re-read the on-disk token inside the recovery lock (so the value passed to `api_start_locked` is the authoritative one) and refuse to clobber a concurrently-started service — bail out and surface the original error instead.

[medium] `needs_clear` is decided inside the lock but `clear_enabled_flag` runs after `drop(g)`. A concurrent `api_start` can race in between: it locks, populates `g`, writes `api-enabled.flag`, releases the lock — and our subsequent `clear_enabled_flag` then wipes that freshly written flag, so the next launch fails to auto-restore a service the user just turned on. Re-acquire the lock and only clear when `g` is still `None` (i.e., no concurrent start has populated it), or accept the race and document it.

[medium] `write_enabled_flag` runs after `drop(g)`, opening a window for a concurrent `api_stop` to empty `g` (and — pre-diff — would have cleared the flag). Our subsequent `write_enabled_flag` then re-creates the flag while `g` is empty, so the next launch auto-restores a service that doesn't exist in memory. Make the flag write idempotent w.r.t. the in-memory state: re-check `g.is_some()` after re-acquiring the lock and only write the flag when state still says running.

[medium] Rollback / recovery paths silently swallow failures (`let _ = write_token_file(&path, old);` and `if api_start_locked(...).is_ok() { write_enabled_flag(&app); }`). A failed rollback leaves the token file out of sync with whatever service is in memory; a failed recovery restart leaves the API stopped. Neither path emits an audit or `eprintln!`, contradicting the mutex-poisoning / SSE-leak audit conventions this file uses everywhere else. At minimum, emit an `audit_event!(.., "api_rotate_rollback_failed", "error" => ..)` (or an `[api_rotate_rollback_failed] …` eprintln) so operators get the same observability they get for poisoned mutexes and leaked SSE writers.

[low] `token` is moved into the closure and `token.clone()` is taken twice on the success-with-running path (once for the unused `NotRunning` arm and once for `api_start_locked(&app, token.clone(), &mut g)`). On the hot path this is one redundant `String` allocation per rotation. Restructure so `token` is moved into `api_start_locked` directly on the `g.is_some()` path (the closure can use `match g { Some(_) => api_start_locked(.., token, ..), None => Ok(RotateOutcome::NotRunning(..)) }` or compute the `NotRunning` info after moving), eliminating the clone on the running-service arm.

TOCTOU between Phase 1 (token load) and Phase 2 (lock): if `api_rotate_token` runs in this window, the in-memory service is rebound to `token_new` (file has token_new after Phase 1) while `api_start`'s alive branch returns `token: Some(token)` with the stale `token_old`. Caller sees a token that no longer authenticates, and `api_start_locked`'s early-return path uses the same stale parameter — the fresh service's actual token never reaches the caller. Pre-refactor this was avoided because `load_or_create_token` ran inside the lock. Consider reloading the token inside the lock (e.g., after the alive check) or storing the active token in `RunningApi` so the alive branch returns the authoritative one.

Phase 1 file I/O runs lock-free, so two concurrent `api_rotate_token` calls are no longer serialized at the state.0 lock (pre-refactor, both `old = read_to_string` and `write_token_file` were inside the lock). Now: A reads `old=T1`, writes `T2`; B reads `old=T2`, writes `T3`; if A's Phase 2 fails after B's Phase 2 commits, A's rollback `write_token_file(&path, old)` clobbers `T3` with `T1`, leaving the in-memory service bound to `T3` and the file at `T1` — state diverges. Low probability but worth either re-serializing the file I/O or capturing `old` after taking the lock.
